Part Three: Refuting the Hidden Root, in two sections. First, the formal argument, in three parts. First, restating the previous refutations to establish a general position.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has said, because it does not see within, it does not reside inside the body; yet because the body and mind know one another and are not separate from each other, it does not exist outside the body."
"I have now reflected and know that it resides in one place.
This pair of statements establishes [the position] separately; the text is clear and easy to understand.
Second, the question concerns what is currently established, and the answer is that it resides in the sense faculties (*indriya*).
The Buddha asked,
"Where is that place now?
Ānanda replied:
"This consciousness that knows the mind neither knows the interior yet can see the exterior; as I ponder it, it must be hidden within the sense organs.
To know the exterior while not knowing the interior—what could this be if not the sense organs?
This refers to the falsely conceptualized consciousness-mind that lies hidden within the five sense organs.
Third, providing an analogy to establish this further extends the principle of its concealment, in two parts:
first, providing an analogy and applying it to the dharma.

"It is like a person who takes a lapis lazuli bowl and places it over both eyes; although there is something covering them, it does not obstruct their vision, and as the faculties perceive, they immediately engage in discernment."
The lapis lazuli is like the sense organ (indriya), and the eye is like consciousness (vijñāna).

Just as the purity of the eye-organ regarding forms does not obstruct the mind—similar to how a lapis lazuli bowl does not obstruct the eye—the mind cognizes each object according to its illumination, following along with the organ.
If this were established, it might seem plausible at first glance; yet upon critical analysis, the corroborative example fails to hold.
Second, establishing it according to principle:
"As for the fact that my conscious mind capable of cognition does not perceive the internal, it is because [the consciousness] resides within the sense organ."
"To see clearly outwardly without obstruction" means that the sense-roots are hidden within.
One merely knows through false conceptualization and fails to realize that faults arise following words; this will be refuted in the following text.
2. Refutation, in two parts:
1. The actual refutation, in three parts:
1. Citing the analogy to establish that both [the seer and the seen] are perceived.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As you have said, that which is hidden within the faculties is like lapis lazuli.
This is a brief summary.
The phrasing is concise, yet it can be understood through the meaning:
"That person will have their eyes covered with a lapis lazuli cage; when they see the mountains and rivers, will they see the lapis lazuli? "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
This person would have lapis lazuli covering their eyes, yet they would actually see the lapis lazuli.
When observing objects from afar and seeing the lapis lazuli up close, the question and answer are fully established; therefore, it is said, “it is thus.”
2. Rebutting the claim by examining its solitary nature according to the Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If your mind were joined with the crystal, you should see the mountains and rivers; why then do you not see your own eyes?”
"In the analogy, both the near and the far are seen; in the dharma (the subject), only the mountains and rivers are seen.
Since the observation of the near has been lost, how can it serve as a valid analogy?
As the dharma and the analogy are unequal, the underlying principle is undermined."
Furthermore, even if one grants the opponent's position, it is refuted so that they have no basis;
thirdly, whether one sees [the eye] or not, both positions fail.
"If one were to see the eye, the eye would be identical to its object, and thus it could not function as a faculty of perception."

If the eye were to see, it would immediately become its own adversary; how then can you claim that it performs conceptualization immediately? This contains the fallacy of contradicting your own words.
If it cannot see, how can you say that this cognition resides within the sense organ, like a crystal vessel?
This concludes the refutation of the fallacy that the dharma and the analogy are inconsistent.
Since these two fallacies have been exposed, the underlying foundation is lost.
Second, the conclusion of the refutation.
"Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious cognition dwells hidden within the sense organs like glass fused with them—is impossible.
4. Refuting [the view] that [consciousness] is internal, in two parts:
1. Establishing [the refutation] by means of the perception of darkness.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I have now further reflected in this way: within the bodies of these sentient beings are the internal organs and viscera, while the orifices reside on the outside; where there are internal organs, there is darkness, and where there are orifices, there is light."
Now, when I open my eyes before the Buddha and see light, it is called seeing the external;
when I close my eyes and see darkness, it is called seeing the internal.
What is the meaning of this?
In this context, the intention is established and the thesis is returned to the internal [self].
Regarding the initial calculation that the mind resides within the body, the Buddha immediately refutes its location within by pointing out that it cannot perceive objects inside the body.
Consequently, he shifted his position to argue that the sense organs are hidden within the body; yet upon exhaustive investigation, he found both views to be untenable.

Reflecting further on the principles of reason, he concluded that the doctrine of their being internal was more consistent with the facts. He thus established the theory that they "conceal darkness and reveal light," thereby refuting the opponent’s fault of claiming that what is internal cannot be perceived.

The seven apertures are clearly exposed and the five viscera are obscure; when the apertures open, they encounter light, and when the eyes close, they face darkness. If light and darkness are perceived, both the internal and external are conditioned by them; therefore, that which is within is certainly free from delusion.
2. Refutation by examining in relation to the eye, in two parts: A.
Refutation through objection, in two parts: 1.
Refuting the prior position, in two parts:
1. A Double Interrogation.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye, or does it not face the eye?”
The interrogation is concluded.
Second, the double refutation, in two parts:
first, the refutation of the counterpart, in two parts: [1a]...
First, that which faces the eye does not belong to the internal.
"If it faces the eye, and darkness is before the eyes, how can it be considered internal?
Facing the eye means being in front; how could what is in front constitute the internal?"
Second, if the external chamber were to become a mass of scorched entrails:
"If it were formed internally, then while dwelling within a dark room devoid of sun, moon, or lamp, that entire darkness within the room would be your own scorched entrails."

If you claim that regardless of sequence, whatever one perceives as darkness is immediately internal, then when you are in a dark chamber devoid of the three luminaries, this chamber which is pitch-black should be your interior, because it is identical to darkness; thus, the scorched viscera would likewise be your interior.
One should formulate the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows:
"Your dwelling in a dark chamber should cause your internal organs to burn, because it is dark; this is identical to your seeing darkness.
Second, the refutation of non-correspondence.
"If it does not face [the object], how can it constitute seeing?
It has never been observed that one sees an object while the visual faculty does not face the objective field.
Second, the refutation of the counter-argument, in two parts:
1. Refuting by citing and overturning the [opponent's] thesis.
"If one is apart from external views, the internal is established in opposition.
This cites the opponent's shifting position.
This argument previously took the darkness of a dark room as an analogy for the darkness before the eyes, concluding that it does not constitute an internal [object].
Fearing that the opponent might argue:
"The darkness I perceive and the darkness of the dark room are two distinct entities."
Why is this? That darkness in the dark room is darkness external to the body; it is called "external seeing" because it is the object perceived when the eyes are open.
The darkness that I see is an internal object; it is called "internal facing" because it is the object perceived when the eyes are closed.

Now, taking the darkness confronted when the eyes are closed and naming it "seeing the internal" is not the same as the darkness seen within a room; how then can one not see that darkness and yet still name it "internal"?
This is therefore a restatement.
However, the various masters' accounts of these views are notably unclear; this is likely due to the translators' skillful abbreviations, which merely provide the restatements.
Let those with wisdom examine this in detail, and do not cling to the coarse hemp of dogmatic adherence.
"If closing the eyes and seeing darkness is called 'within the body,' then when opening the eyes and seeing light, why do you not see your own face?
If you do not see your face, then internal correspondence is not established.
This refutes [the opponent's position].
Even if you grant that one sees within the body by closing the eyes and facing darkness, one should likewise see one's own face by opening the eyes and facing light.
If you allow for the possibility of seeing back toward what is internal and dark, how could you deny the possibility of seeing back toward what is external and bright?
If one is established, all are established; if one is refuted, all are refuted. Therefore it is said: "If the interior face is not perceived, the internal correspondence is not established.
Second, the successive refutation by concession has four parts:
first, being in space, it is not internal, which is identical to the refutation of others.
"If, upon meeting, they were established as such, then this conscious mind and the eye-faculty would reside in empty space; how could they be established as being within?
If they were in empty space, they would not be your own body."

Furthermore, if you maintain that one is able to see the face, then your mind and your eyes must reside in empty space, because seeing is established through the mutual confrontation of the sense faculty and its object.
If you admit they reside in space, this implies they are external; how then can you still maintain that the mind dwells within the body?
Furthermore, if it were in space, it would be the same as that of another person and would naturally not be the substance of your own mind.
Regarding these two fallacies, one should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
Your mental consciousness definitely does not reside within [the body], because you see your own face, just like that of another person.
Regarding the refutation of the subsequent error: simply change the thesis to state that "it is certainly not your substance," with the reason and example as before.
Second, the refutation by showing that the other's view is identical to one's own substance:
"In that case, when the Tathāgata now sees your face, that too must be your body."
If you should maintain that although one sees my face, it is certainly my very self,
then we shall refute this by saying:
since the Buddha also sees you, he too should be your body.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"The body of the Tathāgata is certainly your own substance, because you see his face, just like your own eyes and mind.

If you do not admit that the Buddha's body is yours, then your own eyes and mind are likewise not yours; this would be identical to the previous passage, wherein it was shown that they are not your substance.
3. Refutation through the mutual deficiency of the faculties and the body in cognition:
"If your eye already perceives, then the body, though in contact [with the object], should not have sensation.
Furthermore, if your mind were able to see forms, then the original location of the body should be devoid of cognition, because it would be situated in the space where the visual faculty resides.
If the body possesses sentience, the eye must necessarily lack cognition.
That [sentience] resides in one [of the two] and not in the other; it is not mentioned in the sutra because its phrasing is skillfully concise.
Fourth, the refutation that if both possessed sentience, there would have to be two Buddhas.
"If you insist that the two cognitions of the body and the eye must each have its own consciousness, then your single body would necessarily become two Buddhas.

Since you currently perceive the eye-faculty through self-awareness and experience the location of the body through self-feeling, these are not mutually exclusive; therefore, there must be two minds, for cognition is precisely the mind."
"All who possess a mind shall surely become Buddhas; how could a single body of yours become two Buddhas?

These four successive refutations all arise from the attachments regarding the perceived aspects established within the preceding text. Because deluded sentiments are turbulent and conceptualizations are manifold, they are all thoroughly refuted so that there is nothing left to which one may cling for rescue.
2. Conclusion of the refutation:
"Therefore, you should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called 'seeing the internal' is untenable.
5. Refutation of Conjunction, in two parts:
1. Establishing the argument by citing scripture.
Ānanda said:
"I have often heard the Buddha teach the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise."
This cites the scriptural authority.
Since the eighth *ālayavijñāna* transforms and gives rise to the three objective spheres, it is said that "the mind arises and phenomena arise.
Because the winds of the objective spheres move and can give rise to the waves of consciousness, it is said that "phenomena arise and the mind arises."
Although all [phrases] are cited here, one must take the final phrase—“the arising of mind from the dharma”—as the authoritative basis.

“As I now contemplate, the very essence of this contemplation is my own true mind-nature; wherever it accords with conditions, the mind arises accordingly, yet it does not exist within, without, or in between these three locations.”

Reflecting upon this now, there is indeed the presence of objective conditions and mental engagement; yet, when one investigates where these reside, they are fundamentally non-existent in any of the three locations.

One should know that the mind arises in accordance with its objects; as the mind and object unite, since the objects are not singular, the minds likewise become manifold. This is quite consistent with the Buddha’s words and is certainly no empty discourse.
2. Refuting the Proposition by Analysis, in two parts:
A. The Actual Refutation, in two parts:
1. Refuting the Absence of Essence.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"As for what you have just said—that because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise, and that wherever there is a point of conjunction, the mind follows and exists there"—this restates the previous calculation.
"If this mind has no substance, then there is nothing with which it can conjoin.
Since you have stated that the mind exists because of dharmas, one should know that the mind fundamentally lacks substance;
to say that what lacks substance conjoins is logically impossible.
"How can a single dharma be joined?
This is what is meant.
If that which lacks a substance could be joined, then the nineteen realms would be joined by reason of the seven particles."
This argument is not tenable.

If you stubbornly maintain that an entity lacking substance can undergo conjunction, then the nineteen elements and the seventh sense-object, whose substances are ultimately non-existent, should likewise possess conjunction.
Among the scholars of the world, who would believe that such a thing exists?
Therefore, it is said that this is not so.
Second, the refutation of the existence of an intrinsic nature, in two parts:
I. Refuting the impossibility of internal or external emergence and entry, in two parts:
A. The direct refutation.
"If there were a substantial entity, then as you strike your own body with your hand, does the mind by which you perceive it emerge from within, or enter from without?"
"If it were to emerge from within, one would see it inside the body;
if it were to come from without, one should first see its face.
*Tí* (挃) is pronounced with the *lì* (栗) radical and the *qiè* (切) suffix; it means "to touch."
When the hand touches the body, one must first be aware of it.

Since you claim there is a substantial entity, it cannot be without a locus of rest; thus, the internal and external bases must arise from a single condition, and for this reason, I now interrogate you on both.
The refutation is the same as the previous one.
Second, the refutation of the attempted defense, in two parts:
first, the defense.
Ānanda said:
"To say that 'seeing' is the eye, while the mind's cognition is not the eye, is incorrect in meaning.
This is a shift in his defense.

If one were to argue as in the previous objection that the mind must see forms and so forth, this principle is likely incorrect; for the mind is called "knowing" simply because it is capable of discernment and awareness, whereas the eye is designated as "seeing" only because it possesses the capacity for illumination.
If one were to claim that what the mind knows is what the eye sees, this would certainly be illogical; therefore, it is said to be "unreasonable.
Second, the refutation:
The Buddha said:
"If the eye were able to see, would you be able to see while inside a room?
This is a refutation by means of an analogy.
Just as people in the world who claim to see what is outside must necessarily go out the door before they can be said to 'see'."
If a person resides within a house, can the door see itself?
The door is the eye;
the person is the mind.
Your claim that "the eye sees" is logically unlikely to be so.
If that were the case, then all those who have already died would still possess eyes and should therefore all see objects;
if they do see objects, how can they be called dead?
This refutes the point by citing an actual case.
If it were the eye that is called "seeing," then when a person dies and the eye remains while the mental consciousness has departed from the body, could one say that seeing still exists?
Seeing does not persist in death; in death, there is necessarily no seeing. To claim that seeing resides in the eye—is this not an error!
2. Refutation based on the irrationality of [the self] being either one or many, and either pervasive or localized;
this has two parts: first, the general inquiry: "Ānanda!..."
Furthermore, if this mind of yours that perceives and knows must have a substance, does it consist of a single entity or multiple entities?
Now, as it resides within your body, does it pervade the entire body or does it not pervade the entire body?
"Unity and multiplicity" refer to the essence of mind;
"pervasiveness and localization" refer to the body.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
2. Refutation by way of particulars, in two parts:
1. The fallacy regarding the meanings of being a single entity or multiple entities.
"If it were a single entity, then when you prick one limb with your hand, all four limbs should experience sensation."
"If you perceive it as a whole, then there should be no location for the prick.
If the prick has a specific location, then your 'one body' cannot be established.
This refutes the notion of "oneness."
If the substance of the mind were one, it would be identical across all four locations; thus, when a single limb is touched, all four should simultaneously perceive it.
Even if one were to grant that they all perceive it, the original location of contact would be lost; therefore, it is said to have no fixed location.
If the locus touched by the faculty of cognition were a single entity, how could the principle of multiplicity exist?
If it were multiple entities, then there would be as many persons as there are entities; which entity, then, would be you?
"Your mind is one; how could it be right to say it is many?
If you claim there are many minds, then you yourself must also have multiple bodies."
Among these many bodies, which one is Ānanda?
Therefore, it is asked: "Which body is yours?
Second, the principles of being omnipresent or non-omnipresent are both untenable.
"If it pervades the entire body, it would be the same as what was previously pricked.
This refutes the notion of pervasion.
When one limb is pricked, the other four limbs should also feel it; therefore, it is said to be "the same as before."
"If it were not pervasive, then when you touch your head, you would also touch your feet; while the head would have sensation, the feet should be without cognition.
But this is not the case for you now."
This refutes [the claim that the mind] is not omnipresent.

If you maintain that the mind does not pervade the body, then when tactile sensations from the head and feet occur simultaneously, one part should possess sensation while the other would be unaware of it.
Now you all know this; who could claim that it is not universal?
Therefore, it is said: "Now you are not so.
Second, the conclusion of the refutation.
"Therefore, it should be known that wherever there is a conjunction, the mind would likewise exist; however, such a thing is impossible.
6. Refuting the intermediate [state], in two parts:
first, establishing [the argument] by citing scripture.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When I heard the Buddha conversing with Mañjuśrī and the other Dharma-princes regarding the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the World-Honored One also said:”
"The mind is neither within nor without"—this is the scriptural citation.

As I reflect upon it, there is nothing perceived within, and there is no mutual cognition between the internal and external. Because there is no knowledge within, its existence within is not established; because the body and mind cognize one another, its existence outside is illogical.
This accords with both the teaching and the principle.
As for "not knowing each other," it should rather say "externally they know each other"; I suspect this is a textual error.
Since they now know each other, yet there is no seeing within, they must be situated in between.
This is the correct establishment of the middle [position].
Second, refuting through logical reasoning, which has two parts: first, the refutation itself; second, [the conclusion].
First, the refutation itself: [two parts]. (The text continues.)
I. Regarding the physical location, there are two parts to the sequential refutation:
first, determining its central position.
The Buddha said:
"You speak of the 'middle'; that which is middle must not be confused, nor can it be without a location.
Now, as you investigate this middle, where does it reside?
Does it reside in a place?"
"Does it reside in the body?
If the mind were in the middle [of the body], that middle would have to be free from confusion; yet there must be a specific location—what, then, constitutes the "middle"?
Therefore, by taking the entire body as the locus, one establishes the position of the middle.
2. Refutation according to their specific assertions, in two parts:
1. Refutation by showing that [the self] does not exist within the body.
"If it were in the body, being at the periphery it would not be in the center; being in the center, it would be the same as the interior."
"If you establish the middle position within the body, the body has both a center and an edge; if you reside in the center of the body, how does this differ from being inside?
You ought to perceive the interior."
If it is established in relation to its surroundings, then those surroundings would not be the center; thus, there is the fallacy of contradicting one's own words.
Second, the refutation by way of the uncertainty of location:
"If it exists in a location, does it have something that indicates it, or does it have nothing that indicates it?"
If non-informative action (*avijñapti*) were non-existent, then informative action (*vijñapti*) would lack certainty. Why is this?

For example, when a person uses a marker to designate the center, looking from the east it becomes west, and observing from the south it becomes north; since the substance of the marker is thus indeterminate, the mind should likewise be confused.
If one establishes a middle position regarding external bases of the body, it must necessarily depend on a demonstrable referent; where, then, is this "middle"?
If it cannot be demonstrated, it is ultimately non-existent, just like the horns of a rabbit.
If it were expressible, it would become indeterminate, for one could point toward the east, south, west, or north.
Since that which expresses is thus confused, the mind should likewise be mixed; yet this is logically untenable.
2. Establishing the "Middle" by relying on the sense organs and their objects; this has two parts:
first, the establishment.
Ānanda said:
"Among what I have taught, it is neither of these two kinds.
As the Blessed One said:
'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.'"
"The eye possesses discrimination, while the object of form is devoid of cognition; when consciousness arises between them, that is what constitutes the mind's presence.
The body exists in two aspects, neither of which is established as the self.
Is it not your own venerable teaching that "visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms"?
Now, the middle position is established between the two pillars of the sense organ and the object; it is here that the mind resides.
Because the sense faculties can illuminate their respective objects, they are called "discriminating.
Second, the refutation, which has two parts:
first, the general inquiry.
The Buddha said:
"If your mind were within the sense organs and their objects, would this essence of the mind encompass both, or would it not?
Taking this as the 'middle,' does it still carry along both dharmas—the sense organs and the objects—or is it not so?"
2. Refutation by specific analysis, in two parts:
1. Refuting the combined [position], in two parts:
1.1. If it were combined, it would result in the refutation of confusion.
"If both were combined, the entities of things would become confused.
Because the mind combines them, the faculties and their objects become intermingled; thus, the objects would also possess discernment, and the faculties would also lack consciousness.
"Objects" refer to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*); "essence" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*).
Second, the refutation of the "non-mixed" as being non-central:
"If objects are not the cognition of essence, they stand as opposing entities; how can this be called 'central'?"

"If they are not mixed now, objects would naturally lack cognition, and the substance would naturally illuminate its own objects; thus, they would simply stand as opposing entities. Since there would only be these two aspects, how could a 'middle' exist?"
2. Refuting the position that it does not encompass both.
"If it does not encompass both, it is neither 'knowing' nor 'not knowing'; thus it lacks an essential nature. What, then, could serve as its characteristic?
Because it does not encompass the sense faculties, it is termed "non-knowing."
Because it does not apprehend multiple objects simultaneously, it is not called "non-knowing.
Since both of these meanings are untenable, by what means can the essential nature of the mind be manifested?
If the essential nature does not exist, then the intermediate state itself cannot exist.
2. Conclusion of the refutation:
"Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for [the self] to exist in between.
7. Refutation of non-attachment, in two parts:
First, establishing [the point] by citing a sutra.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
In the past, I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma. He constantly said:
"The nature of the mind that perceives and discriminates is neither within, nor without, nor in between; it has no location whatsoever. Being entirely unattached, this is what is called the mind."
"Then is this non-attachment what is called 'mind'?

Since it is neither internal, external, nor in between, one knows that the mind has nothing to which it is attached; yet one does not realize that the Buddha’s intent was to shatter delusion as having no substance, thereby causing one to recognize the original reality.
As it is said:

"If one seeks the mind throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not found; because the mind is not found, delusion is fundamentally non-existent. Where delusive mind has no place, that is Bodhi; birth-and-death and Nirvana are fundamentally equal."

Failing to understand this meaning, people erroneously point to the text and recklessly establish "non-attachment" as being in accord with the teachings; throughout the world, many practitioners adopt this view.
They claim that at all times being entirely without attachment is their own true mind, yet they do not realize that clinging to this non-attachment is itself a deluded thought.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* states: "That which is mindless is the measure of mind; this I call the measure of mind.
Therefore, the following section refutes it.
Second, the refutation by logical inference has two parts:
I. Refutation, in two parts: A.
Restating the position and posing a dual inquiry.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"You say that the nature of the mind, along with its perceptions and discriminations, has no location whatsoever. Now, regarding all things in the world—such as empty space, water, land, and flying creatures, which are termed 'all'—if you do not cling to them, does this state exist or does it not exist?"

"You say that all things are without attachment and that nothing—whether moving on water, land, or through the air—escapes this. Now, does this mind of non-attachment definitely abide within those various phenomena, or does it not?"
This refers to being currently attached.
Whether [the self] exists or does not exist, both positions entail faults, as will be refuted below.
Second, the successive refutation through logical analysis has three parts:
First, the refutation of [the claim that] it does not abide in non-existence:
"If it were non-existent, it would be the same as a tortoise's hair or a rabbit's horns; how could it then be unattached?
To say it is "non-existent" means it does not abide.

If this determination does not cling to any phenomena, where would there be a mind that is called "non-clinging"? It would then be identical to the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, which ultimately lack any substantial entity.
Since the entity is entirely non-existent, whom do you wish to designate as "non-attached"?
Second, the refutation of the position that there is an entity which constitutes attachment:
"If there were one who is non-attached, he could not be called 'non-existent'."
If this non-attached mind possessed a substantial entity, it could not be said that it is not present in all things;
"non-existence" (wu) is equivalent to "not being present.
Third, by pointing out both faults simultaneously, he concludes and rebukes the preceding error.
"If there is no characteristic,
then there is nothing" refers to the first fault.
"Nothing" means non-existence.
The characteristic is itself all things.
To not abide in the various characteristics is to be without substance, like the horns of a rabbit and so forth.
"It is not that non-existence is the characteristic" points out the subsequent error.
It is not that they lack an essence.
If their essence were necessarily present, it would be present in all things; therefore, it is said to be "identical with characteristics.
If characteristics exist, then [the essence] exists; how could there be non-attachment?
This concludes the previous refutation.
If the marks were to possess a mind, they would be termed "attachment"; how then could you falsely establish the meaning of "non-attachment"?
This is the second conclusion.
"Therefore, you should know that it is impossible for a mind of awakening and cognition to be free from all attachment.
This concludes the seven preceding sections refuting the basis of delusion.
Although the calculations of ordinary minds may differ by ten thousand variations, the basis upon which they rely does not exceed these seven.

To investigate the essence of delusion, one must first destroy its basis; it is like the collapse of a city leading to the death of the enemy, or the overturning of a nest causing the destruction of the eggs.
Although there are seven *viṣayas* (objects), they are only five in terms of their locations, because the fourth and seventh have no distinct locations.
